Jam Session
JAM SESH-un
noun (Boomer slang)
Jam, an informal improvised performance by jazz musicians, is recorded from the late 1920s; jam session appears by the early 1930s in swing-era usage. Rock musicians of the 1960s took it over — long improvised jams were a hallmark of the Grateful Dead, Cream, and the Allman Brothers — and to jam and a jam became common words for any informal music-making (and later, in Gen X and later slang, for a favorite song: "this is my jam").

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A jam session is an informal gathering of musicians who play together without a script, trading solos and building on each other’s ideas — in a 1930s Harlem club, a 1969 rehearsal barn, or a basement with three teenagers and a drum kit. The Christian observation: Scripture is full of music, and a good deal of it sounds like a holy jam. David organized the Levites into bands, and the Chronicler records the musicians "that were instructed in the songs of the LORD, even all that were cunning" (1Ch 25:7) — skilled, trained, and offered to God. The Psalmist asks for both skill and joy: "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise" (Psa 33:3). Psalm 150 calls in the whole band: trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrel, strings, organ, loud cymbals, high sounding cymbals. And the early church’s gatherings had a participatory, every-member quality: "when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm" (1Co 14:26), with the governing rule, "Let all things be done unto edifying." Paul tells the church to teach and admonish "one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord" (Col 3:16). The jam session’s gifts — listening to one another, building on another’s idea, making something together that none could make alone — are body-of-Christ gifts. A family that sings and plays together on a Sunday evening has the best kind of jam session.

Webster 1828 Definition

Swing-era jazz slang (early 1930s), revived by 1960s rock, for an informal improvised gathering of musicians — a shared music-making Scripture honors when skill and joy are offered to God (Psa 33:3; Col 3:16).

JAM SESSION, n. (swing-era slang, early 1930s; revived in 1960s rock) An informal gathering at which musicians improvise together. Also jam (n. and v.). Later: my jam, a favorite song.

Webster (1828) — SESSION, noun [Latin sessio , from sedeo . See Set .] 1. A sitting or being placed; as the ascension of Christ and his session at the right hand of God. 2. The actual sitting of a court, council, legislature, etc.; or the actual assembly of the members of these o rany similar body for the transaction of business. Thus we say, the court is now in session , meaning that the members are assembled for business.

Decode for families: the Presbyterian session (the elders’ court) and the jam session share only a Latin root — both are a "sitting together."

Key Scripture

Psa 33:3 — "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise."

1Ch 25:7 — "So the number of them, with their brethren that were instructed in the songs of the LORD, even all that were cunning, was two hundred fourscore and eight."

Psa 150:3 — "Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp."

1Co 14:26 — "How is it then, brethren? when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine, hath a tongue, hath a revelation, hath an interpretation. Let all things be done unto edifying."

Col 3:16 — "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord."

Modern Corruption

A largely wholesome word; the rock jam culture often surrounded it with drugs, but the practice itself — skilled, shared, improvised music — is something Scripture celebrates when it is offered to God.

expand to see more

The 1960s jam culture had a shadow: the long improvised jam became associated with drug-fueled concerts, and some bands treated the jam as a kind of trance. That shadow belongs to the setting, not to the music. Improvisation is a skill, built on years of practice, and the best jazz and rock musicians brought real discipline to it. Psalm 33:3 asks for exactly that: skill and loudness together.

The church has its own version, and it can recover it. Congregational singing, hymn sings, families making music at home — these are jam sessions in the oldest sense, and they knit people together. Paul’s rule is the right one for any jam: "Let all things be done unto edifying" (1Co 14:26).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Jam (1920s jazz, an improvised performance; perhaps from jam, to press together) + Latin sessio (a sitting) → jam session (early 1930s) → 1960s rock jams.
